description: The mathematics of change and accumulation: the functions it studies, limits, derivatives, integrals, series, differential equations, and calculus in several variables, with the history of how it was assembled. The `calculus` concept itself lives in mathematics.json.

concepts.title: Functions
concepts.summary: A rule that turns each input into exactly one output. Almost everything in calculus is a function: distance over time, temperature along a wire, price against demand. Calculus studies how their outputs change as their inputs do.

concepts.title: Polynomials
concepts.summary: Sums of powers of a variable, like 3x² − 2x + 5. They are the friendliest functions: easy to add, multiply, differentiate, and integrate, and other functions can often be approximated by them, which is the idea behind Taylor series.

concepts.title: Exponential Function
concepts.summary: A function whose growth rate is proportional to its current size, so it doubles at regular intervals. It is the one function that is its own slope, up to a constant multiple, which is why it turns up in populations, interest, decay, and heat.

concepts.title: The Number e
concepts.summary: About 2.71828: the base for which the exponential function has slope exactly equal to its height. It appears as the limit of compound interest with ever finer compounding, and it is as central to calculus as pi is to circles.

concepts.title: Exponential Growth
concepts.summary: Growth in which the increase is proportional to the amount already there: bacteria, viral spread, compound interest. It starts slowly, then overwhelms, which is why people underestimate it. The same curve run backwards describes decay.

concepts.title: Compound Interest
concepts.summary: Interest earned on interest. Each period's gain joins the balance, so the balance grows exponentially, and the more often it compounds the closer it gets to a limit given by e. The rule of 72 estimates the doubling time.

concepts.title: Logarithms
concepts.summary: The inverse of the exponential: it answers 'what power gives this number?'. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition and huge ranges into manageable ones, and were the slide-rule technology of science before computers.

concepts.title: Log Scales
concepts.summary: Scales where each step multiplies rather than adds: decibels, the Richter scale, pH, star magnitudes. They fit quantities spanning many orders of magnitude onto one readable axis, and match how hearing and sight respond to intensity.

concepts.title: Trigonometry
concepts.summary: Sine, cosine, and tangent: the relationships between angles and lengths in triangles, extended to any angle by going round a circle. They describe anything that repeats: waves, orbits, vibrations, alternating current.

concepts.title: The Unit Circle
concepts.summary: A circle of radius one centered at the origin. The point at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), which is the cleanest way to see what sine and cosine are and why they repeat every full turn.

concepts.title: Radians
concepts.summary: Measuring angles by the length of arc on a circle of radius one, so a full turn is 2π. It looks odd but makes the calculus clean: in radians, the slope of sine is exactly cosine, with no stray constants.

concepts.title: The Sine Wave
concepts.summary: The smooth, endlessly repeating curve traced by sine. It is the shape of a pure tone, of a swinging pendulum's motion, and of the alternating current in a wall socket, and any repeating pattern can be built from sums of them.

concepts.title: Inverse Functions
concepts.summary: A function that undoes another: the logarithm undoes the exponential, the square root undoes squaring. Their graphs mirror across the diagonal, and the slope of an inverse follows neatly from the slope of the original.

concepts.title: Composition
concepts.summary: Feeding the output of one function into another: f(g(x)). Complicated behavior is built from simple pieces chained together, and the chain rule of calculus exists to differentiate exactly this.

concepts.title: Hyperbolic Functions
concepts.summary: Sinh, cosh, and tanh: built from exponentials, and to the hyperbola what sine and cosine are to the circle. A hanging chain takes the shape of a cosh curve, and tanh is a favorite squashing function in neural networks.

concepts.title: Limits
concepts.summary: What a function's value approaches as its input approaches something, even if it never gets there. The idea that makes 'instantaneous' and 'infinitely many small pieces' precise, and the foundation under derivatives and integrals.

concepts.title: Epsilon–Delta
concepts.summary: The rigorous definition of a limit: for every tolerance ε around the answer there is a distance δ around the input that keeps the output within it. It replaces vague 'gets closer' with a challenge you can win or lose.

concepts.title: Continuity
concepts.summary: A function is continuous when you can draw its graph without lifting the pen: small changes in input give small changes in output. Formally, the limit equals the value. It underlies the guarantee that things do not jump.

concepts.title: Intermediate Values
concepts.summary: A continuous function that goes from below zero to above zero must cross zero somewhere between. It sounds obvious and is what guarantees that equations have solutions, and it underlies root-finding methods.

concepts.title: Discontinuities
concepts.summary: The ways a function can break: a hole, a jump, a vertical asymptote, or wild oscillation. Classifying them shows which can be repaired and which cannot, and tells you where calculus's usual tools stop working.

concepts.title: Infinitesimals
concepts.summary: Quantities smaller than any positive number yet not zero. Newton and Leibniz used them freely, critics ridiculed them, and limits replaced them for two centuries until a rigorous version returned in the twentieth century.

concepts.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
concepts.summary: When a limit comes out as 0/0 or ∞/∞, take the ratio of the derivatives instead. It turns an inscrutable quotient into a plain one, and shows that in these standoffs it is the rates of change that decide.

concepts.title: Squeeze Theorem
concepts.summary: If a function is trapped between two others that approach the same value, it must approach that value too. It handles tricky wobbling functions, such as x·sin(1/x), by pinning them between simple bounds.

concepts.title: Asymptotes
concepts.summary: A line a curve approaches ever more closely without touching it: the vertical line where 1/x blows up, or the horizontal line a curve settles toward. They show what a function does at its edges.

concepts.title: Indeterminate Forms
concepts.summary: Expressions like 0/0, ∞ − ∞, or 1^∞ whose value cannot be read off from their pieces, because the answer depends on how fast each piece moves. Resolving them is a main use of limits.

concepts.title: Derivatives
concepts.summary: The instantaneous rate of change: how fast a quantity is changing right now. Geometrically the slope of the tangent line, physically speed. It is the first of calculus's two big ideas, and it turns curves into something you can compute with.

concepts.title: Rates of Change
concepts.summary: How much one quantity changes per unit change of another: miles per hour, dollars per year, degrees per meter. Average rates are easy; calculus asks what happens when the interval shrinks to nothing.

concepts.title: Tangent Lines
concepts.summary: The straight line that just touches a curve at a point and has the same direction there. Its slope is the derivative. Zoomed in far enough, any smooth curve looks like its tangent line.

concepts.title: Motion
concepts.summary: Position, velocity, and acceleration: each is the derivative of the one before. Speed is how fast position changes; acceleration is how fast speed changes. This chain was calculus's first great triumph, and the reason it was invented.

concepts.title: Differentiation Rules
concepts.summary: A handful of rules that turn finding a derivative from a limit each time into mechanical routine. Power, product, quotient, and chain rules cover nearly every function you will meet.

concepts.title: Power Rule
concepts.summary: The derivative of xⁿ is n·xⁿ⁻¹: bring down the power, then lower it by one. The simplest and most used rule, and it handles roots and reciprocals too, since they are powers in disguise.

concepts.title: Product Rule
concepts.summary: The derivative of f·g is f′g + fg′. When two changing things multiply, each contributes its own change while the other holds still. Think of a rectangle whose width and height both grow.

concepts.title: Quotient Rule
concepts.summary: The derivative of f/g is (f′g − fg′)/g². It follows from the product rule and the fact that 1/g has its own derivative, and it is the rule people misremember most often.

concepts.title: Chain Rule
concepts.summary: The derivative of a function inside a function multiplies the rates: the outer rate at the inner value, times the inner rate. If a car goes twice as fast as a bike and the bike four times as fast as a walker, the car is eight times.

concepts.title: Autodiff
concepts.summary: Computing exact derivatives of a program by applying the chain rule to each elementary step as it runs. Backpropagation, the engine of neural network training, is a special case, and it makes gradients cheap for millions of parameters.

concepts.title: Implicit Differentiation
concepts.summary: When y is tangled up with x in an equation, like x² + y² = 25, differentiate both sides and solve for the slope. It gives the slope of a circle at any point without first solving for y.

concepts.title: Related Rates
concepts.summary: If several changing quantities are linked by an equation, their rates are linked too. Differentiate the relationship with respect to time to find how fast a ladder's top slides down as its foot slides out.

concepts.title: Optimization
concepts.summary: Finding the best value: the most profit, the least material, the shortest path. For smooth functions the best is where the slope is zero, so calculus turns 'best' into 'solve derivative equals zero'.

concepts.title: Critical Points
concepts.summary: Places where the derivative is zero or undefined: the tops of hills, bottoms of valleys, and flat spots. Candidates for maxima and minima, which need a further test to tell them apart.

concepts.title: Mean Value Theorem
concepts.summary: Somewhere between two points on a smooth curve, the instantaneous slope equals the average slope. If you averaged 60 mph on a trip, at some moment you were doing exactly 60. Many of calculus's proofs rest on it.

concepts.title: Second Derivative
concepts.summary: The derivative of the derivative: how fast the slope itself is changing. It measures curvature and, in motion, acceleration. A positive second derivative bends up like a bowl; a negative one bends down like a cap.

concepts.title: Concavity
concepts.summary: Whether a curve bends up or down. Concave up holds water; concave down spills it. The second derivative tells which, and the sign tells whether a flat spot is a valley or a peak.

concepts.title: Inflection Points
concepts.summary: Places where a curve changes from bending one way to the other, like the middle of an S. They mark where growth switches from speeding up to slowing down, such as the middle of an epidemic curve.

concepts.title: Linear Approximation
concepts.summary: Near a point, a smooth function behaves like its tangent line, so you can estimate values with simple arithmetic. It is the first term of the Taylor series and the basis of much of physics and engineering.

concepts.title: Newton's Method
concepts.summary: Find where a function is zero by guessing, drawing the tangent, jumping to where the tangent crosses zero, and repeating. It typically doubles the number of correct digits each step and is how calculators find square roots.

concepts.title: Integrals
concepts.summary: Accumulation: adding up infinitely many infinitely thin slices to get a total, such as area under a curve, distance from speed, or work from force. The second big idea of calculus, and the reverse of differentiating.

concepts.title: Riemann Sums
concepts.summary: Approximate an area by slicing it into thin rectangles and adding them. Make the slices thinner and the sum approaches the exact area: that limit is the integral. It is the definition that everything else rests on.

concepts.title: Numerical Integration
concepts.summary: Approximating an integral by computer when no formula exists, using trapezoids, parabolas, or clever sampling. Most integrals of real-world functions cannot be done by hand, so this is how most integrals actually get computed.

concepts.title: Antiderivatives
concepts.summary: A function whose derivative is the one you started with. Running differentiation backwards, it comes with an arbitrary constant, since constants vanish when you differentiate. Finding one is the hard part of integrating.

concepts.title: Fundamental Theorem
concepts.summary: The link that makes calculus one subject: accumulating a rate of change gives the total change. To find an area, find an antiderivative and subtract its values at the ends. Differentiating and integrating are inverses.

concepts.title: Integration by Parts
concepts.summary: The product rule read backwards: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. It swaps a hard integral for an easier one, and is the standard tool for products like x·eˣ or x·sin x.

concepts.title: Substitution
concepts.summary: The chain rule read backwards: rename a tangled inner expression as a single variable, integrate, then rename back. It undoes a change of variable and is the first technique to try on any integral.

concepts.title: Trig Substitution
concepts.summary: For integrands containing √(a² − x²) and similar, let x be a sine, tangent, or secant. The square root collapses into a trigonometric identity, and the geometry of a right triangle does the rest.

concepts.title: Partial Fractions
concepts.summary: Split a complicated fraction of polynomials into a sum of simple ones you can integrate one by one. It is algebra done to make calculus possible, and it also unlocks inverse Laplace transforms.

concepts.title: Improper Integrals
concepts.summary: Integrals over infinite ranges or of functions that blow up. A limit decides whether the area is finite, which yields surprises: some infinitely long shapes have finite area, and some slowly decaying ones have none.

concepts.title: Solids of Revolution
concepts.summary: Spin a curve around an axis and it sweeps out a solid. Slice it into thin disks or shells and integrate to find the volume. It is how you find the volume of a vase, or derive the cone and sphere formulas.

concepts.title: Arc Length
concepts.summary: The length of a curve, found by adding up tiny straight segments, each the hypotenuse of a small horizontal and vertical step. It shows how integration measures things that are not straight, and why the answers so often involve square roots.

concepts.title: Series
concepts.summary: Adding infinitely many terms. Sometimes the sum settles on a finite number and sometimes it runs away, and telling which is the central question. Series are how calculus writes functions as endless polynomials.

concepts.title: Sequences
concepts.summary: An ordered list of numbers that goes on forever: 1, 1/2, 1/4, and so on. The question is where it is heading, which is a limit again, now over the position in the list. Every series is a sequence of running totals.

concepts.title: Convergence
concepts.summary: A series converges when its running total approaches a fixed number. Terms must shrink toward zero, but that alone is not enough, since the harmonic series shrinks and still grows without bound.

concepts.title: Geometric Series
concepts.summary: Each term is a fixed multiple of the last: 1 + ½ + ¼ + …. It converges to a/(1 − r) when the ratio r has size less than one. It is the simplest infinite sum, and the model most others are compared with.

concepts.title: Zeno's Paradoxes
concepts.summary: Achilles can never catch the tortoise, because he must first reach where it was, and it will have moved. The paradox stood for two millennia until infinite series showed that infinitely many steps can add up to a finite time.

concepts.title: The Harmonic Sum
concepts.summary: 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + … has terms shrinking to zero, yet the sum grows without bound, though very slowly: it takes over 12,000 terms to reach 10. The classic warning that shrinking terms are not enough.

concepts.title: Convergence Tests
concepts.summary: A toolkit for deciding whether a series converges without summing it: compare it to a known series, or use ratios, integrals, or alternating signs. Each test works in some cases and is silent in others, so choosing among them is a craft.

concepts.title: Power Series
concepts.summary: An infinite polynomial, a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + …. Inside its radius of convergence it behaves like an ordinary function and can be differentiated and integrated term by term, which makes it a powerful way to represent and compute functions.

concepts.title: Radius of Convergence
concepts.summary: How far from its center a power series still converges. Inside the radius it works; outside it diverges. The radius is set by the nearest trouble spot of the function, even a complex-number one you cannot see on the real line.

concepts.title: Taylor Series
concepts.summary: Rebuild a function near a point from its derivatives there: value, slope, curvature, and so on, each adding a term. It explains how calculators compute sine and eˣ, and it turns hard functions into polynomials.

concepts.title: Euler's Identity
concepts.summary: e^(iπ) + 1 = 0: five fundamental constants in one line. It falls out of the Taylor series for the exponential, sine, and cosine, and shows that growth and rotation are two faces of the same function.

concepts.title: Fourier Series
concepts.summary: Any repeating pattern can be built from a sum of sines and cosines of different frequencies. It is the mathematics of decomposing a sound into its tones, and the root of signal processing and compression.

concepts.title: Differential Equations
concepts.summary: Equations that describe how something changes, and ask what it must therefore be. Newton's laws, heat flow, populations, circuits, and epidemics are all written this way, so much of physics and engineering is differential equations.

concepts.title: ODEs
concepts.summary: Differential equations with one independent variable, usually time: a swinging pendulum, a decaying isotope, a cooling cup of coffee. Their solutions are functions of time whose shape follows from the rule.

concepts.title: PDEs
concepts.summary: Equations involving rates of change in several variables at once, such as time and position. They describe waves, heat, fluids, and quantum states, and are harder to solve, so many are understood only through computation.

concepts.title: Separable Equations
concepts.summary: Sort the variables to opposite sides of the equation, so all the y stuff is on one side and all the x stuff on the other, then integrate both. The first solving technique for differential equations, and enough for growth and decay.

concepts.title: Laplace Transform
concepts.summary: Turns a differential equation into an algebra problem by trading functions of time for functions of a complex variable. Engineers use it to analyze circuits and control systems, then transform the answer back.

concepts.title: Euler's Method
concepts.summary: Solve a differential equation step by step: from where you are, follow the slope a short way, recompute the slope, and repeat. Crude but general, it is the ancestor of the numerical solvers behind weather forecasts and simulations.

concepts.title: Initial Values
concepts.summary: A differential equation plus a starting state. The rule says how things change; the initial condition picks which of the infinitely many possible histories actually happens. Under mild conditions, exactly one does.

concepts.title: Harmonic Oscillator
concepts.summary: Anything pulled back toward a resting position in proportion to how far it is displaced: springs, pendulums, atoms in a lattice. The equation gives sine waves, and it shows up everywhere small vibrations do.

concepts.title: Predator and Prey
concepts.summary: Rabbits multiply, foxes eat rabbits, foxes starve, rabbits recover. Two coupled equations produce endless cycles, an early example of using differential equations to model an ecosystem.

concepts.title: Logistic Growth
concepts.summary: Growth that starts exponentially but levels off at a carrying capacity as resources run out, making an S-shaped curve. It models populations and the spread of ideas, and in its discrete form it turns chaotic.

concepts.title: Heat Equation
concepts.summary: Describes how temperature spreads: heat flows from hot to cold at a rate proportional to the difference. Sharp features smooth out, and the equation is the mathematical face of diffusion and of the arrow of time.

concepts.title: Wave Equation
concepts.summary: Describes how disturbances travel: plucked strings, sound, water, light. Solutions are shapes moving at a fixed speed without changing form, and standing waves are the notes a string or drum can play.

concepts.title: Navier–Stokes
concepts.summary: The equations of fluid motion: air over a wing, water in a pipe, weather. They are the basis of modern flow simulation, and whether smooth solutions always exist in three dimensions is one of the unsolved million-dollar problems.

concepts.title: Schrödinger Equation
concepts.summary: The equation that governs how a quantum wave function changes with time. It predicts the energy levels of atoms and much of chemistry, and its solutions give probabilities, not certainties, for what you will measure.

concepts.title: Maxwell's Equations
concepts.summary: Four equations that describe electricity, magnetism, and light as one thing. Varying electric fields make magnetic ones and vice versa, giving waves that travel at the speed of light, and the equations underlie all electronics.

concepts.title: Multivariable Calculus
concepts.summary: Calculus for functions of several inputs: temperature over a map, height over terrain, a fluid's velocity everywhere. Slopes become directions, areas become volumes, and it is the mathematics of fields and surfaces.

concepts.title: Partial Derivatives
concepts.summary: How a function changes when you nudge one input and hold the rest still: how the temperature changes as you move east, ignoring north and altitude. Each input gets its own slope.

concepts.title: The Hessian
concepts.summary: The grid of all second partial derivatives, describing curvature in every direction. At a flat spot it tells you whether you are at a peak, a valley, or a saddle, and it guides second-order optimization.

concepts.title: The Gradient
concepts.summary: The vector of all partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest climb, with a length equal to how steep it is. Follow it uphill to a peak, or the reverse to a valley.

concepts.title: Directional Derivatives
concepts.summary: The rate of change of a function along any chosen direction, not just along the axes. It is the gradient's dot product with that direction, which is why the gradient gives the steepest one.

concepts.title: Gradient Descent
concepts.summary: Minimize a function by repeatedly stepping downhill along the negative gradient. It is how neural networks learn: measure the error, find which way lowers it, take a small step, repeat billions of times.

concepts.title: Multiple Integrals
concepts.summary: Integrals over areas or volumes, built by integrating one variable at a time. They give total mass from density, volume under a surface, and probability over several variables.

concepts.title: The Jacobian
concepts.summary: The matrix of partial derivatives of a change of coordinates. Its determinant says how much the change stretches or shrinks area or volume locally, which is why it appears whenever you switch variables in a multiple integral.

concepts.title: Coordinate Systems
concepts.summary: Different ways of labeling points: grid coordinates, polar with distance and angle, cylindrical, spherical. The right choice can turn an ugly problem into an easy one, as a circle is simple in polar and awkward in grid.

concepts.title: Vector Fields
concepts.summary: An arrow attached to every point in space: wind on a weather map, the pull of gravity, the flow of a river, an electric field. They describe how something pushes or flows at each place.

concepts.title: Divergence
concepts.summary: How much a vector field spreads out from a point: a source has positive divergence, a sink negative, and steady incompressible flow zero. It measures the net outflow per unit volume.

concepts.title: Curl
concepts.summary: How much a vector field swirls around a point. Put a tiny paddle wheel in the flow and the curl says how fast and about which axis it turns. A field with no curl comes from a potential.

concepts.title: Line Integrals
concepts.summary: Add up a quantity along a curve: the work done by a force along a path, or the mass of a wire with varying density. In a conservative field the answer depends only on the endpoints.

concepts.title: Surface Integrals
concepts.summary: Add up a quantity over a curved surface: the flow of water through a net, or the flux of a field through a sphere. It is a double integral adapted to a surface that need not be flat.

concepts.title: Green's Theorem
concepts.summary: Adding up the microscopic swirl inside a region equals the circulation around its boundary. A line integral around a loop becomes an area integral, and vice versa, the first of the great boundary theorems.

concepts.title: Stokes' Theorem
concepts.summary: The total swirl of a field across a surface equals the circulation around the surface's edge. It generalizes Green's theorem to curved surfaces and is a key step in relating Maxwell's equations to their integral forms.

concepts.title: Divergence Theorem
concepts.summary: The total outflow through a closed surface equals the total divergence inside it. Whatever is created within must leave through the skin, which is the mathematical form of conservation laws such as that of charge.

concepts.title: Lagrange Multipliers
concepts.summary: Optimize something subject to a constraint: at the best point on the constraint, the gradient of the objective lines up with the gradient of the constraint. The multiplier also says how much the optimum would gain if the constraint loosened.

concepts.title: History of Calculus
concepts.summary: From Greek areas and Indian series to Newton and Leibniz, calculus was assembled over two thousand years, put on shaky footing, and made rigorous in the nineteenth century. Its history shows how ideas outrun their proofs.

concepts.title: Archimedes
concepts.summary: The Greek mathematician who found areas and volumes by slicing shapes into ever thinner pieces and squeezing between bounds, nearly two thousand years before calculus. His method anticipated integration, and he found the area of a parabolic segment.

concepts.title: Isaac Newton
concepts.summary: Developed his method of fluxions in the 1660s to describe motion and gravity, then used it to explain planetary orbits. He saw derivatives as speeds and integrals as sums of motions, and wrote it up late and reluctantly.

concepts.title: Gottfried Leibniz
concepts.summary: Independently invented calculus in the 1670s and 1680s, and gave it the notation still used: the integral sign ∫ and dy/dx. His symbols make the rules nearly automatic, which is much of why his version spread.

concepts.title: The Priority Dispute
concepts.summary: Newton and Leibniz each invented calculus and each was accused of copying. The quarrel split English and continental mathematics for a century, and English notation lagged as a result.

concepts.title: The Analyst
concepts.summary: Bishop Berkeley's 1734 attack on the foundations of calculus, mocking infinitesimals as 'ghosts of departed quantities'. He was right that the arguments were unclear, and the criticism spurred the search for rigor.

concepts.title: Real Analysis
concepts.summary: The rigorous rebuilding of calculus on limits and the real numbers, mostly by Cauchy and Weierstrass in the nineteenth century. It replaced intuition with careful definitions and revealed strange things, such as continuous functions with no slope anywhere.
